etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English him, from Old English him, from Proto-Germanic *himmai (“to this, to this one”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian him (“him”), West Frisian him (“him”), Sylt North Frisian ham, höm (“him”), Dutch hem (“him”), German Low German hum, hüm, em (“him”), German ihm (“him”, dative).

definitions.definition: With dative effect or as an indirect object. [from 9th c.]

quote.text: […] therfoꝛ Chꝛiſt wold not call him abominable / But the verye abomination it ſilf.

quote.text: ‘I promise,’ he said as I gave him the papers.

definitions.definition: With accusative effect or as a direct object. [from 12th c.]

quote.citation: 1852 March – 1853 September, Charles Dickens, Bleak House, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: ‘He's got it buttoned in his breast. I saw him put it there.’

definitions.definition: A masculine pronoun; he as a grammatical object.
(colloquial) As a grammatical subject or object when joined with a conjunction.

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Acts:
quote.text: Apon a daye apoynted, the kynge arayed hym in royall apparell, and set hym in his seate, and made an oracion unto them.

quote.citation: 1765, Oliver Goldsmith, The traveller, or, A prospect of society:
quote.text: Though poor the peasant’s hut, his feasts though small,He sees his little lot the lot of all;[...]But calm, and bred in ignorance and toil,Each wish contracting, fits him to the soil.

definitions.definition: With nominative effect: he, especially as a predicate after be, or following a preposition. [from 15th c.]
